draft.title: Sources and quotations in a text
card: A source is where a writer got information. A quotation uses the exact words of a person or document, usually inside quotation marks.
Writers quote experts and name their sources to make a text seem reliable. A named source suggests the claim has backing.
Readers should check who the source is. Does the person have training or experience in the topic? Could they gain from the reader believing them?
A named source does not make a claim true. A reliable source is usually an expert on the topic, is named, and has no strong reason to mislead.
draft.remember: Quoting and citing make a text seem reliable, so check who the source is.

a.q: Why does a writer quote a named marine scientist in an article about coral reefs?
opts: To make the claims seem more reliable
To prove every claim in the article is true
To make the article shorter and simpler
To show the writer has no opinion on reefs
a.why: A named expert makes the claims seem backed by knowledge. It does not prove them true, because readers still need to check the source.
a.clue: Think about what an expert's name adds to a claim.

b.q: An article says a new snack is healthy. It quotes Dale, who owns the company that makes the snack. What should a careful reader think?
opts: Dale may gain from the claim, so check other sources
Dale is named, so the claim must be reliable
Dale is quoted, so the claim has been proven true
Dale's words are exact, so they cannot be biased
b.why: Dale owns the company, so he could gain if readers believe him. A careful reader checks other sources. Being named or quoted exactly does not make a claim reliable.
b.clue: Ask whether the source could gain from being believed.

a.best: To make the claims seem more reliable

b.best: Dale may gain from the claim, so check other sources

problems.detail: The right option is the only hedged one ('may'), while the others all use absolute words ('cannot', 'proven', 'must'). It is also slightly longer, and it echoes the clue's wording ('gain'). A student could pick it without knowing the idea.

b.q: An article says a new snack is healthy. It quotes Dale, who owns the company that makes the snack. What should a careful reader think?
opts: Dale earns money from sales, so check other sources
Dale is named, so readers can trust the claim
Dale is quoted exactly, so the claim is proven
Dale runs the company, so his word settles it
b.why: Dale earns money if people buy the snack, so he has a reason to praise it. A careful reader checks other sources. Running the company is tempting, but it gives him a stake in the claim, not training in health.
b.clue: Think about Dale's reason for praising the snack.
